title: Choosing the Right Measure of Central Tendency

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The choice among mean, median and mode rests on two things: the variable’s scale of measurement (recall §1.1.2) and the shape of its distribution.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Given a real dataset, which one do you report? First ask what scale the variable is on; that rules measures in or out. Then, for interval or ratio data, ask whether the distribution is roughly symmetric or skewed (skewed means one tail is longer than the other; §3.9 measures it).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
• Nominal data (blood group) → mode only; mean and median are undefined.
  • Ordinal data (cancer stage, Kuppuswamy class) → median (and mode). The mean is not valid, though it is sometimes used pragmatically.
  • Interval/ratio data, roughly symmetric (height in a healthy population) → mean. It uses every value, and for Normal data (the bell-shaped curve of §5.7.2.2) it varies less from sample to sample than the median does (the property called efficiency in §7.1.1). With heavier tails than the Normal the advantage can shrink or reverse.
  • Interval/ratio data, skewed or with outliers (household income, hospital length of stay) → median, which resists the distortion the mean suffers.
  • Positive, right-skewed data whose logs are roughly symmetric (antibody titres) → geometric mean (§2.2.3).

points.html: Two independent checks drive the decision: scale of measurement (nominal → mode; ordinal → median; interval/ratio → mean usually appropriate) and, for interval/ratio data, shape (symmetric → mean; skewed → median).

Classic exam and thesis trap: reporting a mean (and SD) for an ordinal or a strongly skewed variable (income, length of stay, many laboratory values) when the median (and IQR, §3.4) is the better summary.

A quick shape check: in a unimodal distribution, a mean noticeably away from the median usually signals skew. The converse is weaker. Mean and median can be close in a distribution that is bimodal, or skewed in a way that balances out, so look at a histogram (§4.3.1) before trusting either number alone (von Hippel, 2005).

The same two checks, scale and shape, return when choosing between parametric tests (tests that assume a particular distribution for the data, such as the t-test in §9.2) and non-parametric tests (§10.1).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 2.2

questions.prompt: Hospital length of stay is right-skewed. In one ward the mean stay is 6.2 days and the median is 4 days. Which would you report as the typical stay, and why could the mean alone mislead?
questions.answer: Report the median, 4 days (with the IQR). A few very long stays pull the mean up to 6.2 days, above what most patients experience: at least half of them stay 4 days or less. The mean remains useful for a different question, total bed-days (mean × number of patients), but it does not describe a typical patient.

questions.prompt: For a dataset of blood groups (A, B, AB, O), which single measure of central tendency is valid, and why do the other two fail?
questions.answer: Only the mode. Blood group is nominal: its categories have no numeric values to average and no order to find a middle in, so the mean and median are undefined. The mode just reports the commonest category.

questions.prompt: Haemoglobin of 50 pregnant women at a PHC is grouped as 7 to <9 g/dL (6 women), 9 to <11 (14), 11 to <13 (20) and 13 to <15 (10). Compute the grouped mean, median and mode. Then check the mode against the empirical relation mode ≈ 3 × median − 2 × mean.
questions.answer:
Mid-points 8, 10, 12, 14; h = 2; N = 50; cumulative frequencies 6, 20, 40, 50.

Mean = (6×8 + 14×10 + 20×12 + 10×14) ÷ 50 = (48 + 140 + 240 + 140) ÷ 50 = 568 ÷ 50 = 11.36 g/dL.

Median: N/2 = 25 falls in 11 to <13 (cumulative 40). L = 11, cf = 20, f = 20. Median = 11 + [(25 − 20) ÷ 20] × 2 = 11 + 0.5 = 11.5 g/dL.

Mode: modal class 11 to <13 (f₁ = 20), f₀ = 14, f₂ = 10. Mode = 11 + [(20 − 14) ÷ (40 − 14 − 10)] × 2 = 11 + (6 ÷ 16) × 2 = 11.75 g/dL.

Empirical relation: 3 × 11.5 − 2 × 11.36 = 34.5 − 22.72 = 11.78 g/dL, within 0.03 of the formula mode. The order mean < median < mode usually indicates, in single-peaked data, a slight left skew: a longer tail toward low haemoglobin.
